questions.prompt: The rate of simple diffusion for a lipid-soluble substance across a cell membrane is limited by an intrinsic Vmax  once the concentration gradient becomes sufficiently high.
In a cell where the Na^+/K^+  ATPase is chemically inhibited, the resulting dissipation of the sodium gradient will cause the cell to lose water and shrink.
According to the force-velocity relationship in skeletal muscle, hypertrophy of individual muscle fibers increases the maximum velocity of shortening (Vmax ).
Mechanical power generated by a skeletal muscle is at its maximum value when the muscle is performing a maximal isometric contraction.
During postrotatory nystagmus following a clockwise spin (to the right), the fast, saccadic component of the eye movement is directed to the left.
In the vestibular hair cells, bending of the stereocilia away from the kinocilium results in membrane hyperpolarization and a decrease in the firing rate of the associated sensory nerve.
A complete lesion of the right optic tract will result in a visual defect characterized as left homonymous hemianopia.
The fovea centralis is the area of the retina with the highest sensitivity for vision in low-light (scotopic) conditions due to its high density of rods.
An inhibitory postsynaptic potential (IPSP) is physiologically generated when a neurotransmitter increases the membrane permeability to Cl^-or K^+ .
Activation of α1 -adrenergic receptors on vascular smooth muscle by norepinephrine typically results in widespread vasodilation to increase tissue perfusion.
Stimulation of the parasympathetic nervous system causes a negative dromotropic effect on the heart, which is reflected as an increase in the PR interval on an ECG.
Pulmonary surfactant increases the surface tension of the fluid lining the alveoli to provide the elastic recoil necessary for expiration.
In an upright individual, the ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) ratio is significantly higher at the apex of the lung than at the base.
The peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid bodies significantly increase their firing rate only when the arterial partial pressure of oxygen (PaO2 ) drops below 60 mmHg.
Arterial hypoxemia caused by a significant intrapulmonary right-to-left shunt is easily corrected by having the patient breathe 100% oxygen.
During strenuous aerobic exercise in a healthy athlete, the arterial PO2decreases significantly while the arterial PCO2  increases to drive hyperventilation.
According to the Frank-Starling Law, an acute increase in ventricular preload causes an upward and leftward shift of the cardiac function curve.
The closure of the semilunar (aortic and pulmonary) valves marks the beginning of the isovolumetric relaxation phase of the cardiac cycle.
The third heart sound (S3 ) is a normal physiological finding in children and is associated with the rapid ventricular filling phase of diastole.
Sympathetic venoconstriction increases the "unstressed" blood volume in the venous reservoir, thereby decreasing the mean systemic filling pressure and venous return.
During heavy exercise, the total peripheral resistance (TPR) increases significantly because of the widespread sympathetic activation of α1  receptors in systemic arterioles.
Glomerulotubular balance is an intrinsic renal mechanism that adjusts the rate of sodium and water reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule to match changes in GFR.
Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) increases the water permeability of the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle by inserting aquaporins into the luminal membrane.
The "aldosterone escape" phenomenon in states of primary mineralocorticoid excess is largely mediated by pressure natriuresis resulting from ECF volume expansion.
Renin is released from juxtaglomerular cells in response to a decrease in the chloride concentration in the tubular fluid at the macula densa.
The filtration fraction represents the portion of the renal plasma flow that is filtered across the glomerular capillaries and is calculated as GFR divided by RPF.
Renal compensation for chronic respiratory acidosis involves an adaptive increase in the renal excretion of filtered bicarbonate to lower the plasma pH.
Acetazolamide, a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor, promotes the development of metabolic acidosis by inhibiting the reabsorption of filtered bicarbonate in the proximal tubule.
Cholecystokinin (CCK) is the primary hormone responsible for the coordinated contraction of the gallbladder and the relaxation of the sphincter of Oddi during a meal.
Secretin acts on pancreatic ductal cells to stimulate the secretion of a bicarbonate-rich fluid that neutralizes acidic chyme in the duodenum.
The rate of gastric emptying is significantly slowed by the presence of a high concentration of fatty acids or hypertonic solutions in the duodenum.
The cephalic phase of gastric secretion, which can be triggered by the thought or smell of food, is mediated primarily by the vagus nerve.
The majority of bile salts are reabsorbed via active transport in the proximal duodenum to be recycled via the enterohepatic circulation.
Migrating motility complexes (MMCs) are periodic contractions that clear the gut of remnants during fasting and are primarily inhibited by the hormone motilin.
Duodenal S cells are responsible for the endocrine release of cholecystokinin (CCK) in response to the presence of dietary fats and amino acids.
Growth hormone (GH) secretion is characterized by a strong inhibitory response to exercise, starvation, and deep sleep.
Insulin prevents postprandial hyperkalemia by stimulating the Na^+/K^+  ATPase to move potassium from the extracellular fluid into the cells.
Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease) is characterized by low plasma cortisol levels and an appropriately low plasma ACTH level.
Parathyroid hormone (PTH) increases the renal reabsorption of calcium in the distal tubule while simultaneously decreasing the reabsorption of phosphate in the proximal tubule.
Oxytocin is synthesized in the anterior pituitary gland and is responsible for milk ejection and uterine contractions.
The mid-cycle LH surge that triggers ovulation is an example of positive feedback, where rising estrogen levels stimulate the anterior pituitary.
Cortisol exerts a "permissive" effect on vascular smooth muscle, which is necessary for the normal vasoconstrictor response to catecholamines.
Type II diabetes mellitus is fundamentally characterized by a down-regulation or resistance of insulin receptors in target tissues like skeletal muscle and fat.
The Cushing reflex is a compensatory response to increased intracranial pressure and is clinically recognized by the triad of hypertension, tachycardia, and hyperventilation.
Acclimatization to high altitude involves an adaptive leftward shift of the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve due to an increase in 2,3-DPG production.
The hyperventilation observed during strenuous exercise is primarily driven by a significant increase in the mean arterial partial pressure of carbon dioxide (PaCO2 ).
In the acute response to severe hemorrhage, the baroreceptor reflex causes a decrease in total peripheral resistance (TPR) to maintain blood flow to the skin and gut.
During a fever, the hypothalamic thermoregulatory center is reset to a higher set-point temperature, making the body feel "cold" at normal room temperature.
In a patient with metabolic alkalosis caused by persistent vomiting, the kidneys effectively compensate by producing a highly alkaline urine.
Severe diarrhea typically produces a metabolic acidosis characterized by a normal plasma anion gap and an elevated plasma chloride concentration.
